title: Cross-Functional Leadership in Digital Transformation: Impact on ERP and HCM Implementation Success
summary: This paper investigates the role of cross-functional leadership in driving successful Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and Human Capital Management (HCM) system implementations during digital transformation initiatives. Digital transformation requires an integrated approach, where leaders coordinate across functions to align strategies and foster an adaptive culture. Utilizing a mixed-method approach that includes quantitative data analysis and case studies, this study analyzes how cross-functional teams contribute to better ERP and HCM project outcomes, such as on-time delivery, cost efficiency, and user adoption. Findings suggest that cross-functional leadership, characterized by collaborative, adaptable, and strategic skills, is a critical factor in overcoming project challenges and achieving implementation success. Organizations pursuing digital transformation should prioritize building cross-functional teams with strong leadership to maximize ERP and HCM benefits.

title: Digital Transformation and Business Portfolio Reconfiguration: Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation
summary: Digital conversion is re-understanding the limits between telecommunications, media, and entertainment sectors, presenting new chances for well-established telecom companies to broaden their operations outside of traditional connectivity offerings. This research probes into the relationship between digital transition and business portfolio enhancement via a case analysis of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation (NTT). Based on the theories regarding dynamic capabilities, digital business model innovation, and platform ecosystems, this study shows how NTT employs its network infrastructure, customer communication channels, and data resources to organize entertainment-related services. The analysis pinpoints four beneficial operating mechanisms: accessing end-customers through communication services, achieving personalized service backed by data, creating superior entertainment experiences enabled by technologies, and facilitating integrated service transactions. In the meantime, four significant challenges are found. There is competition over resources between the telecom and entertainment sectors. Disputes emerge in organizational frameworks and corporate cultures. The company depends significantly on external content suppliers, and its business portfolio becomes overly diversified. This research proposes several solutions, such as cross-business cooperation frameworks, combined units for technological and content innovation, graded portfolio management, inter-departmental performance assessment systems, and enhanced data governance. The study reaches the conclusion that sustainable value generation cannot be accomplished solely via technology investment. Enterprises are required to dynamically integrate digital capabilities, organizational resources, and portfolio strategies within a unified ecosystem.

title: Digital Transformation Processes in Large Infrastructure Owners: An Organizational Change Perspective
summary: Abstract Large infrastructure owners (LIOs) own and operate the critical infrastructure that underpins modern society. Under growing demands for efficiency and resilience, digital transformation (DT) entailing both technological and organizational change has become a strategic necessity for LIOs to sustain service delivery. The change process of DT in LIOs unfolds under the competing demands of digital initiatives and high-reliability operations, which converge on organizational members expected to enact the initiatives while upholding uninterrupted services. However, existing studies on DT in LIOs have concentrated on technology adoption, and broader DT process research leaves unexplained how members come to enact transformation. To address these gaps, this study focuses on the internal change process of DT in LIOs, examining how organizational strategies deepen member engagement across stages. Adopting an organizational change lens and a cross-level process framework that spans organizational and individual levels, we trace how organizations reshape established arrangements to bring members into DT. Through a single-case study of a Chinese airport group, we identify three stage-specific strategic mechanisms: establishing legitimacy under authoritative leadership, enacting safety-first logics in technology and organizing, and embedding identity change among members. A member-centric process model is then abstracted, conceptualizing DT progression as a recursive process advanced through deepening member engagement under specific contextual conditions. This study contributes to research on DT in LIOs by delineating how they sequence and adapt their strategies to realize systemic DT, enriches the broader DT literature by tracing DT progression through member engagement, and advances organizational change research by elucidating the recursive interplay between strategies and member responses that sustains DT as continuous change. Practically, advancing DT in LIOs requires drawing legitimacy and capabilities from outside the organization, while deriving opportunities from continuous operations and creating authorized space for digital work within them.

title: Digital Transformation in Human Resources: Examining Oracle HCM Cloud’s Role in Project Management
summary: In recent years, digital transformation has reshaped Human Resources (HR), transitioning it from a traditionally administrative field to a strategic cornerstone of organizational development. Oracle Human Capital Management (HCM) Cloud, a leading HR management solution, has emerged as a critical tool in facilitating this transformation. Its role in project management within HR includes optimizing workflows, increasing data transparency, and enabling strategic insights. This paper explores the functionalities and impacts of Oracle HCM Cloud in HR project management, highlighting its benefits in workforce planning, data analytics, compliance, and employee engagement. Through a review of recent literature and case studies, this research underscores Oracle HCM Cloud’s potential to enhance HR project management efficiency and adaptivity in a dynamic business environment.

title: Oracle HCM Cloud as a Catalyst for Digital Transformation in HR: A Review of Case Studies
summary: This paper investigates the impact of Oracle HCM Cloud on the digital transformation of Human Resource (HR) functions, focusing on various case studies across industries. In today’s fast-evolving business landscape, organizations are increasingly adopting cloud-based HR solutions to streamline processes, improve data-driven decision-making, and enhance the employee experience. Oracle HCM Cloud, with its robust suite of applications, plays a crucial role in facilitating this transformation. Through a comprehensive review of case studies, this paper examines how organizations have successfully implemented Oracle HCM Cloud to address challenges in talent management, employee engagement, and operational efficiency. Results indicate that Oracle HCM Cloud offers substantial benefits in terms of process automation, data integration, and user accessibility. However, the study also identifies challenges related to change management and data privacy. Ultimately, the findings suggest that Oracle HCM Cloud can significantly contribute to building a future-ready HR model that aligns with organizational goals.

title: Human resource development through ESG-oriented agricultural training: Knowledge outcomes in IoT-assisted and conventional irrigation settings
summary: Background: The social pillar of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) emphasizes human resource development, yet evidence on ESG-oriented agricultural training in non-farming urban communities remains limited. This study assesses changes in knowledge following an ESG-oriented agricultural training program and examines whether IoT-assisted infrastructure is associated with differential knowledge gains. Methods: A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design without a control group was employed among 20 female community beneficiaries across two sites in Batam, Indonesia, Barelang (IoT-assisted drip irrigation) and Nongsa (conventional irrigation). A purpose-built 25-item binary (yes/no) self-assessment instrument was administered before and after training, covering four domains; land preparation, plant maintenance, IoT and smart farming, and digital marketing. Participant baseline characteristics were collected separately. Findings: Mean scores increased significantly from 10.70 (SD = 4.71) to 22.20 (SD = 2.33) out of 25 (W = 210.0, p-value < 0.001). Plant maintenance and digital marketing showed substantial gains increasing from 11.7% to 93.3% and from 35.0% to 94.0% suggesting that applied training was accessible across educational backgrounds. However, the IoT domain diverged sharply: Barelang gained +3.35 items of 5 reaching near-perfect comprehension, while Nongsa declined by −0.33 items, which may indicate a possible response-shift phenomenon whereby theoretical instruction without hands-on technology exposure heightened awareness of knowledge limitations rather than consolidating applied competency. The small sample (n = 20) limits generalisability. Conclusion: Participants reported significantly higher self-assessed knowledge after ESG agricultural training regardless of educational diversity, while IoT-related outcomes appeared to differ by infrastructure access. Novelty/Originality of this article: This study contributes to the ESG literature by examining whether IoT infrastructure access is associated with human resource.

title: AI AND CORPORATE GOVERNANCE IN INDIA: EXAMINING DIRECTORS' DUTIES, FIDUCIARY RESPONSIBILITIES AND LIABILITY FOR AI-ASSISTED DECISIONS
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support corporate decisions involving finance, compliance, recruitment, risk assessment, cybersecurity and business strategy. These tools can improve speed and help directors process large amounts of information, but they can also produce inaccurate, biased or difficult-to-explain recommendations. This creates a central corporate-law question: when a director relies on an AI-generated recommendation, does that reliance satisfy the director's existing legal duties, and who should be accountable if the decision causes harm? This paper examines the question through a doctrinal and comparative legal method. It analyses the Companies Act, 2013, particularly section 166, relevant principles emerging from Indian decisions on directors' fiduciary obligations and oversight and selected regulatory approaches to AI governance. It argues that Indian company law already provides a meaningful foundation for accountability through duties of good faith, care, diligence, independent judgment and avoidance of conflicts of interest. Those duties do not disappear when a company uses technology. However, the application of traditional standards to opaque or probabilistic AI systems raises practical questions about reasonable reliance, explainability, documentation and board-level supervision. The paper recommends a proportionate, risk-based approach: directors should not be strictly liable merely because an AI-assisted decision fails, but they should be expected to understand material risks, test important outputs, preserve meaningful human judgment and ensure appropriate oversight. The aim should be responsible innovation rather than either unrestricted automation or a blanket prohibition on AI-assisted governance.

title: Preventing Corporate Disputes Through Family Settlements: An Interdisciplinary Analysis of Family Law and Corporate Governance in India
summary: Family-owned businesses play a significant role in India, but when matters of succession, ownership, and/or management of the business become corporate disputes, the continuity of the family business is threatened. Family settlements are a recognised way to settle disputes about family property and multiple claims, but their utility as tools for preventing disputes has been relatively underdeveloped in the context of family-owned businesses. This article aims to explore whether family settlements can serve as a governance mechanism to prevent potential family conflicts within family-owned businesses. It examines the legal principles applicable to family settlements and their application in Kale v Deputy Director of Consolidation and Ram Charan Das v Girja Nandini Devi and their interplay with the Companies Act, 2013 and corporate governance. A carefully drafted family settlement sets clear expectations regarding succession provisions, co-ownership, involvement in management, shareholder voting on decisions, and resolution mechanisms for disputes within the family. Such settlements, however, cannot replace the mandatory corporate law, the company's constitution, or the rights of non-family shareholders. The article thus urges a perspective of family settlements as an additional layer of family governance, which can contribute to resolving family conflicts before they reach the level of corporate litigation. The article shows how to integrate family law concepts into corporate governance, thereby proposing to avoid conflict and controversy within the family business by establishing structured and forward-looking agreements.

title: Maritime Chokepoints and Business Exposure
summary: Maritime chokepoints connect concentrated transport routes with economic activities beyond shipping. This working paper examines how geographical disruption becomes organisational exposure and identifies conditions supporting preparedness among businesses and public authorities. The analysis develops a conceptual framework informed by institutional studies of maritime transport and trade resilience. It distinguishes direct shipping dependence from exposure mediated through suppliers, customers and supporting services. Route geography is examined alongside contracts, inventories, delivery schedules and information flows to explain why organisations can experience different consequences from the same disruption. Time is treated as a determinant of exposure. Delays affect production, stock availability, working capital and service obligations in different ways. The paper therefore considers the complete cost of delivery rather than freight charges alone. Inventory buffers, alternative routes and contractual remedies are assessed as conditional resources whose usefulness depends on duration, feasibility and operational requirements. Four dimensions structure the proposed framework: dependency knowledge, temporal preparedness, practical alternatives and decision coordination. These dimensions connect supply relationships with critical time limits, realistic substitution options and responsibilities for action. Early warning is examined as a process of translating developments into organisational consequences, supported by staged decisions rather than fixed predictions. Three hypothetical illustrations address a specialised manufacturing input, a time sensitive exporter and replenishment for an essential service. They clarify possible transmission mechanisms without estimating losses or forecasting route closures. Comparative research is proposed around defined functions, using procurement records, interviews, continuity plans and exercises where suitable evidence is available. The paper contributes a bridge between maritime geopolitics, supply chain resilience and business decision making. Its practical value concerns integrated procurement, finance, operational planning and public warning arrangements. The framework remains untested and does not assess named companies or current voyage safety. Subsequent research should investigate which combinations of knowledge, alternatives and authority support effective organisational responses.

title: ESG Practices and Financial Performance With the Moderating Role of the Sustainability Committee
summary: ABSTRACT This paper examines whether sustainability committee presence strengthens the association between ESG practices and corporate financial performance. Drawing on stakeholder theory and agency theory, the paper argues that ESG practices may be financially relevant when supported by board‐level monitoring, but may remain symbolic when oversight is weak. Using an international panel of publicly listed firms from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America and Australia over 2015–2024, the analysis applies baseline and moderation panel models with industry, year and country fixed effects. Corporate financial performance is measured using return on assets, return on equity and Tobin's Q. ESG practices are measured using Bloomberg ESG scores and pillar scores. The findings show that ESG practices are positively associated with financial performance, with stronger evidence for return on assets and Tobin's Q than for return on equity. The ESG × SCOM interaction is positive, although its statistical significance varies across financial performance measures and model specifications, providing cautious support for the moderating role of sustainability committee presence.

title: From ecosystem conditions to sustainable performance: role of dynamic capability and digital transformation in MSMEs
summary: Purpose Despite entrepreneurial ecosystems (EE) being viewed as enablers of competitiveness and performance, the firm-level mechanism through which EE conditions translate into sustainable outcomes remains ambiguous, particularly in manufacturing micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs). This study aims to examine the effect of EE conditions on sustainable performance (SP), and effect of dynamic capability (DC) as a mediating mechanism and digital transformation (DT) as a boundary condition moderator. Design/methodology/approach This study uses cross-sectional survey data from 257 manufacturing MSMEs in an emerging market such as India. EE conditions are modelled as a second-order formative construct, estimated using the disjoint two-stage approach. The hypothesized relationships were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), with predictive relevance assessed using PLSpredict. Findings The findings show that EE conditions exert a significant positive effect on both DC and SP. DC significantly influences SP and partially mediates the EE−SP relationship. The interactions between DT and EE significantly strengthen the EE−SP relationship, confirming DT’s role as a boundary condition. Practical implications MSMEs aiming for sustainable outcomes should focus on developing DC alongside ecosystem engagement. Digital preparedness should be viewed as an enhancement of overall capabilities rather than a separate performance driver. Furthermore, policy interventions should integrate digital readiness into broader ecosystems, rather than treating the two separately. Originality/value This study contributes to the research on EE and DC capability theory by examining the EE−SP relationship in the MSME context, which is jointly controlled by an internal capability mechanism and a digital contingency condition.

title: Independent Green Innovation, Shareholder Concentration, Supervisory Pay and Firm Performance – Evidence from China
summary: This study examines the relationships between independent green innovation, shareholder concentration, supervisory compensation, and firm performance among Chinese listed companies. Using panel data from the CSMAR database covering 2003–2020, the study applies panel regression methods to investigate firm performance measured by return on assets (ROA). The empirical results indicate that independent green innovation is negatively associated with ROA, while shareholder concentration and supervisory compensation exhibit positive associations with firm performance. These findings contribute to the understanding of how corporate sustainability initiatives and governance mechanisms relate to financial performance in China's emerging market context. title: Negotiating Digital Innovation and Pesantren Traditions: Teachers’, Administrators’, and Students’ Experiences of Digital Transformation in Islamic Religious Education
summary: Transformasi digital di pondok pesantren bukan tentang memperkenalkan perangkat teknologi atau memindahkan pembelajaran ke platform online, melainkan negosiasi antara peluang teknologi, pengetahuan agama, otoritas guru, pedagogi tatap muka, dan nilai-nilai institusi. Makalah ini mengkaji pengalaman dan proses negosiasi pembelajaran PAI di sebuah pondok pesantren di Indonesia menggunakan desain studi kasus kualitatif (18 informan yang dipilih secara purposif: enam guru PAI, dua manajer pendidikan, dan 10 siswa). Data dikumpulkan melalui wawancara semi-terstruktur, delapan sesi observasi kelas non-partisipan, dan analisis dokumen pembelajaran institusi; dianalisis secara tematik menggunakan familiarisasi data, pengkodean awal, pengembangan kategori, dan interpretasi lintas sumber. Temuan diorganisir menjadi empat dimensi analitis yang saling terkait: adopsi teknologi digital, adaptasi pedagogis, mediasi guru, dan negosiasi berbasis nilai. Presentasi, materi audiovisual, dan smartphone memperluas akses ke materi pembelajaran dan mendiversifikasi aktivitas pembelajaran tetapi tidak menggantikan penjelasan langsung, diskusi, interaksi guru-siswa, dan praktik pembelajaran yang ada. Guru memediasi informasi agama digital dengan seleksi, pemeriksaan, penjelasan, dan kontekstualisasi sumber. Informan juga menyebutkan gangguan, kredibilitas informasi online, kompetensi digital guru, dan waktu persiapan tambahan. Penelitian ini menjelaskan transformasi digital sebagai negosiasi kontekstual (bukan pergeseran linear dari pembelajaran tradisional ke digital). Penelitian ini menawarkan lensa analitis empat dimensi untuk memahami interaksi antara penggunaan teknologi, keputusan pedagogis, mediasi pengetahuan keagamaan, dan nilai kelembagaan pesantren. Kerangka ini bersifat interpretatif dan berakar pada satu kasus sehingga perlu dikaji lebih lanjut dalam konteks kelembagaan yang berbeda. The rapid expansion of digital technology has transformed educational practices, including Islamic Religious Education (IRE) in Islamic boarding schools. However, the integration of technology into pesantren education presents a particular challenge because technological innovation must be negotiated with established pedagogical practices and religious values. This study aims to examine how technology-driven transformation occurs in IRE at Pondok Pesantren Al-Kifyah Riaty and how teachers and students negotiate the relationship between digital innovation and traditional Islamic educational practices. A qualitative case study was employed involving 18 participants, consisting of six IRE teachers, two educational administrators, and ten students. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and analysis of relevant institutional documents and were analyzed thematically through data reduction, coding, categorization, and cross-source triangulation. The findings reveal four interconnected dimensions of digital transformation: digital adoption, pedagogical adaptation, teacher mediation, and value-based negotiation. Digital technologies expanded access to learning resources, diversified teaching strategies, and supported student engagement; however, technology did not replace direct instruction, teacher–student interaction, or traditional Islamic learning practices. Teachers increasingly acted as selectors, evaluators, and mediators of digital religious information, while challenges emerged concerning teachers’ digital competence, student distraction, information credibility, and additional preparation time. The study contributes a context-sensitive understanding of digital transformation in Islamic education by demonstrating that meaningful digitalization in pesantren is not a linear transition from traditional to digital learning, but a negotiated process in which technological innovation is integrated with pedagogical, cultural, and religious values.

title: IMPLEMENTASI INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL REPORTING STANDARDS (IFRS) PADA PELAPORAN KEUANGAN UMKM DI KOTA MAKASSAR DALAM MENGHADAPI PERSAINGAN GLOBAL
summary: Penelitian ini mengkaji implementasi International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), yang diadopsimelalui SAK EMKM dan SAK EP, pada praktik pelaporan keuangan UMKM di Kota Makassar di tengah persainganglobal yang semakin intensif, serta mengevaluasi faktor determinan dan implikasinya terhadap daya saing.Penelitian menggunakan desain campuran sequential explanatory, menggabungkan survei terhadap 387responden UMKM yang valid melalui stratified random sampling dengan wawancara semi-terstruktur terhadap 24informan purposive, dianalisis melalui regresi berganda dan analisis tematik enam tahap.Rata-rata indeks implementasi IFRS hanya 34,2 dari skala 100. title: User-Centric Design Thinking Framework for Digital Transformation: Bridging the Digital Literacy Gap in Thai Manufacturing SMEs
summary: While digital transformation is essential for enhancing the competitiveness of Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs), a significant barrier remains in the form of low levels of employees' digital literacy. This study addresses this critical challenge by proposing and validating a User-Centric Design Thinking Framework for developing digital tools in environments characterized by varying levels of technological proficiency. Using a Thai manufacturing SME as a case study, the study employed a five-stage Design Thinking process involving 20 participants to develop a web-based production management system. The methodology emphasized empathy and iterative feedback to ensure the system was intuitive, accessible, and aligned with user needs. Post-implementation analyses revealed substantial operational improvements, including an 81.1% reduction in production monitoring time and an 80.7% decrease in reporting time, accompanied by significant cost savings. Usability testing, incorporating both qualitative feedback and quantitative assessment, demonstrated a high level of user satisfaction (mean score = 4.52 out of 5). The findings indicate that a user-centric approach is effective in not only bridging the digital literacy gap but also enhancing business performance. This study provides a practical and replicable framework for technology adoption in SMEs and contributes to the broader understanding of inclusive digital transformation in developing economies.

title: The Evidentiary Value of Commercial Books - Between Legal Requirements and Digital Transformation in the Saudi Legal System: A Critical Analytical Study
summary: This research examines commercial books under the Saudi legal system through an analytical and critical study of their statutory regulation and evidentiary value. It aims to clarify the concept of commercial books, the scope of the obligation to maintain them, their types, and the requirements governing their regularity and preservation. The study also addresses the legal regulation of electronic commercial books and the extent to which it keeps pace with the digital transformation taking place in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The research further discusses the evidentiary value of commercial books in favor of and against merchants under the Saudi Law of Evidence, with particular attention to the statutory conditions for relying on such books, the effect of their regularity or irregularity, and the role of the court in examining them and assessing their probative value. The study adopts analytical and critical approaches by examining the relevant statutory provisions and evaluating their suitability for the contemporary commercial environment. The research concludes that the Saudi legal framework provides, in general, a clear system governing commercial books and their evidentiary value, while also recognizing the use of electronic means for recording and preserving commercial data. Nevertheless, the study identifies a need to further develop certain provisions, particularly those relating to the criteria for the obligation to maintain commercial books, the regulation of electronic books, the integrity of digital data, and the traceability of any amendments made to such data. The study recommends updating certain provisions of the Commercial Books Law, strengthening coordination between it, the Law of Evidence, and the Electronic Transactions Law, and adopting more detailed rules governing digital commercial books in a manner that keeps pace with modern technological developments, enhances the stability of commercial transactions, and strengthens the evidentiary value of commercial books before the courts.

title: Digital Transformation Of The Construction Supply Chain: Whole-process Green Supply Chain Management With China Construction E-Commerce Co., Ltd(Cloud Building Network)As The Industry Benchmark
summary: Construction supply chain management mainly cooperates with the whole process of raw material procurement, component production, logistics transportation to the site for construction, operation and maintenance, and integrates information flow, logistics and capital flow,so as to achieve the best goal of project cost, duration and quality. In recent years, the research and practice in this field have changed from the previous linear integration to the common development of platform, intelligence, and Greening Based on digital technology. Taking China Construction E-Commerce Co. , Ltd (Cloud Building Network) as an example, this paper analyzes the digital transformation of the construction supply chain. It mainly studies the changes caused by the innovation and development of CSCEC e-commerce cloud building in this field, including the integrated service ecology of bidding, supplier quotation, online contract signing, delivery and receipt. Cloud Building Network can deeply assist in the construction supply chain, promote green supply chain management to achieve a full-process closed loop, and reach the goal of sustainable development. This article summarizes the hot research directions in the field and analyzes the impact of digital transformation on efficiency, effectiveness, and innovation ecosystem structure, in order to inspire future development directions.

title: The Impact of Managerial Myopia on Corporate Green Innovation
summary: Whether managerial myopia shapes corporate green innovation has attracted surprisingly little attention. This paper examines that question directly. Evidence comes from 33,813 firm-year observations on 4,661 A-share firms listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen between 2010 and 2021, and the analysis covers three issues: the effect of managerial myopia on green innovation, the mediating channels of strategic alliances and R&D investment, and the moderating role of digital transformation. Managerial myopia turns out to hold green innovation back. A large part of the damage is indirect: myopic managers are less inclined to build alliances with other firms and they cut R&D spending, and both shifts dampen green innovation. Digital transformation pulls in the other direction, weakening the negative myopia-green innovation link and easing the myopia-alliance and myopia-R&D relationships as well. By placing managers' psychological traits at the center of the analysis, this paper enriches work on the antecedents of green innovation and offers firms practical guidance for green transformation and sustainable development.

title: Secure SDLC Practices in Financial Application Development
summary: The financial services sector is a highly regulated and security-sensitive industry that increasingly relies on software applications to deliver core services such as digital banking, online trading, mobile payments, and financial data analytics. However, the rise of cyber threats, regulatory compliance mandates, and evolving user expectations have amplified the need for embedding security into every stage of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). Secure SDLC (SSDLC) practices provide a structured framework for ensuring that financial applications are designed, developed, tested, and deployed with security as a fundamental principle rather than an afterthought. This paper explores the significance of SSDLC in financial application development, reviewing theoretical frameworks, industry practices, and empirical studies. It outlines major methodologies such as threat modeling, static and dynamic code analysis, secure coding standards, DevSecOps integration, and compliance-driven validation. Furthermore, it analyzes case studies from global banks and fintech companies to demonstrate how SSDLC practices mitigate risks like fraud, unauthorized access, data breaches, and regulatory violations. The study adopts a mixed-method methodology combining systematic literature review and practical insights from industry implementations. Results highlight that organizations that adopt SSDLC practices achieve measurable improvements in vulnerability reduction, faster compliance audits, and enhanced consumer trust. Ultimately, the paper argues that SSDLC adoption in financial systems is not only a technological necessity but also a strategic enabler of resilience, trust, and long-term competitiveness.

summary: The article examines institutional, regulatory and human-capital prerequisites for the digital transformation of internal audit in Uzbekistan’s public sector. Drawing on Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 100 of 13 March 2026 and international guidance issued by the IIA, INTOSAI, OECD, IMF and World Bank, it develops a conceptual framework connecting digital infrastructure, risk-based procedures, professional training and performance measurement. The paper proposes a practice-based auditor training mechanism with a sandbox environment, a digital competency matrix and measurable implementation indicators. The study is conceptual and documentary; no unverified empirical effects are claimed

title: Recognizing the Rights of the Ozone Layer: A proposal for ecological integrity, legal innovation and sustained global action
summary: Recognising the Rights of the Ozone Layer: A Proposal for Ecological Integrity, Legal Innovation and Sustained Global Action This policy brief, published by the Association for Environmental Protection and Sustainable Development (AEPSD), Cameroon, examines the scientific, legal and policy foundations for strengthening the protection of the Earth’s ozone layer through innovative approaches to international environmental governance. Building upon the achievements of the 1985 Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer and the 1987 Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, the brief explores the possibility of recognising the ozone layer’s ecological integrity as a legally protected interest within an evolving international environmental law framework. While acknowledging the significant progress achieved in reversing ozone depletion, the publication argues that continued scientific monitoring, international cooperation, precautionary regulation and effective compliance mechanisms remain essential to safeguarding the ozone layer for present and future generations. The brief further advances AEPSD’s call for global emergency-level commitment to environmental protection, emphasising that such advocacy does not imply the existence of a formally declared international environmental emergency. Particular attention is given to the responsibilities and opportunities of developing countries, including those in Africa, regarding environmental governance, financial assistance, technology transfer and institutional capacity building. The publication concludes with policy recommendations directed at governments, international organisations, research institutions and civil society actors. title: Corporate Governance and Financial Performance of Food and Beverage Companies in Nigeria
summary: This study examines the relationship between corporate governance and the financial performance of listed food and beverage companies in Nigeria. An ex post facto research design was adopted, using secondary data extracted from the annual reports of 10 listed companies over the period 2016–2025. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and panel regression techniques, including pooled ordinary least squares, fixed effects and random effects. Financial performance was measured using return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE), while corporate governance was represented by board size, board independence, board meetings, board diversity, audit committee meetings, audit type and audit report lag. The reported results indicate that board size has a significant positive relationship with financial performance, whereas board independence exhibits a significant negative relationship. Board meetings, board diversity, audit committee meetings, audit type and audit report lag generally show statistically insignificant relationships with performance. Leverage is positively and significantly associated with ROE in the reported model. The study highlights the importance of effective board composition and oversight in promoting financial performance among listed food and beverage companies in Nigeria.

title: Digital Corruption and Business Performance in the Digital Economy
summary: Digital corruption has become an important governance issue in the digital business environment. The increasing use of digital platforms, electronic payment systems, e-government services, and information technology has improved transparency and efficiency, but it has also created new opportunities for fraud, bribery, data manipulation, and misuse of digital systems. This study aims to examine the development of research on digital corruption and business performance through a bibliometric and literature review approach. Data were collected from Scopus-indexed publications during the 2017–2023 period using keywords related to digital corruption and business performance. The search identified nine publications, but only seven articles were directly relevant to the topic after screening based on title, abstract, and research focus. The findings show that research on digital corruption and business performance remains limited and fragmented. Most studies focus on digital transformation, e-government, institutional effectiveness, digital payment, and anti-corruption mechanisms, while firm-level studies remain scarce. The review also indicates that digital transformation and digital payment systems can reduce corruption by improving transparency, traceability, accountability, and monitoring. However, weak governance, poor cybersecurity, and limited internal control can turn digital systems into new channels for corrupt practices. This study contributes to the literature by positioning digital corruption as a strategic business governance risk that can affect financial performance, operational efficiency, innovation, stakeholder trust, and organizational sustainability. Future research should empirically examine the relationship between digital corruption and business performance in sectors with high digital transaction intensity, such as banking, financial technology, education, e-commerce, accounting services, and public procurement.

title: Modern slavery governance, digital transformation and financial distress risk: evidence from legally grounded text-based accounting measures
summary: Purpose This paper aims to develop and validate a legally grounded accounting measurement framework for modern-slavery governance and examines whether the resulting governance measures are associated with firms' financial distress risk. Existing research predominantly relies on ESG ratings, disclosure proxies, or qualitative assessments that do not clearly distinguish externally specified governance obligations from firms' disclosed governance architecture. We address this measurement gap by translating mandatory modern-slavery governance requirements into reproducible firm-level accounting measures and evaluating their informational relevance for accounting-based risk assessment. Design/methodology/approach This research adopts a two-corpus measurement framework. The first corpus comprises mandatory modern-slavery legislation and internationally recognised institutional frameworks issued between 1930 and 2024, including the Tariff Act (1930), California Transparency in Supply Chains Act, UK Modern Slavery Act, French Duty of Vigilance Law, Australian Modern Slavery Act, German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, Norwegian Transparency Act, the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), and complementary institutional frameworks including the ILO, OECD, PRI, and the United Nations Guiding Principles. Rather than serving as institutional background, these sources are used to define the governance construct by identifying legally codified organisational obligations and harmonising them into a unified governance ontology representing implementation-oriented governance mechanisms.The second corpus comprises more than 5,000 annual reports of S&P 500 firms covering the period 2010–2022. Artificial intelligence (AI), natural language processing (NLP), and supervised machine-learning techniques operationalise the predefined governance ontology to identify disclosed evidence of implementation-oriented governance mechanisms within corporate reports, thereby generating firm-year Modern Slavery Index (MSI) measures. A complementary Digital Transformation Index (DTI) captures disclosed digital capability. The empirical design combines firm and year fixed-effects estimation with 2SLS endogeneity-sensitivity analysis and additional tests addressing disclosure intensity and boilerplate reporting, institutional validity, digital-capability interactions, competing explanations and potential mechanisms. Findings The findings show that firms disclosing stronger implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance mechanisms exhibit lower financial distress risk, although the strength of this association varies across the underlying institutional architectures. Among the four governance measures, the California-based MSI2 provides the strongest evidence, indicating that disclosed governance mechanisms centred on supplier verification, monitoring, accountability, and supply-chain oversight are associated with lower financial distress risk. Digital transformation, by contrast, does not independently reduce financial distress risk and is associated with lower Altman Z-scores in several specifications, a pattern consistent with – but not establishing – the organisational costs and implementation challenges that may accompany technological transformation. Importantly, digital capability also conditions the association between disclosed modern-slavery governance and financial distress risk, with the positive MSI4 × DTI interaction indicating that the financial relevance of governance disclosure varies with firms' digital capabilities under particular institutional arrangements. Overall, the findings indicate that legally grounded measures of disclosed modern-slavery governance contain economically relevant information for financial-distress assessment, while their associations vary across governance architectures and according to firms' digital capabilities. Originality/value This paper makes four contributions to the accounting literature. First, it develops four transparent, legally grounded, and fully reproducible Modern Slavery Indices (MSI1–MSI4), each derived from distinct regulatory and institutional governance frameworks, providing researchers, practitioners, managers, auditors, and policymakers with standardised accounting measures of implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance. Second, it introduces a novel two-corpus measurement framework that explicitly separates construct definition from empirical observation by deriving the governance construct from mandatory legislation and internationally recognised frameworks before operationalising it through AI-enabled textual analysis of corporate reports. Third, it demonstrates how artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and supervised machine-learning techniques can operationalise externally defined governance obligations into scalable firm-level accounting information while preserving construct validity. Finally, it provides evidence that these legally grounded accounting measures contain decision-useful information for accounting-based risk assessment, advancing research on non-financial accounting measurement, governance architecture, disclosure credibility, internal control systems, and corporate resilience under emerging mandatory reporting regimes.

title: Audit Quality, the Fraud Diamond, and Fraudulent Financial Reporting: The Moderating Role of the Audit Committee in Indonesia's Consumer Sector
summary: Background: Fraudulent financial reporting is relatively infrequent but disproportionately costly, and recent fraud evidence continues to show the importance of detecting material misstatement risk (Association of Certified Fraud Examiners). Indonesian consumer cyclicals and non-cyclicals are analytically relevant because intense competition, performance targets, macroeconomic exposure, and long distribution chains can increase reporting pressure. Objective: This study tests the effects of audit quality and the fraud diamond on fraudulent financial reporting risk and examines audit committee activity as a moderator. Methods: The sampling frame comprised Indonesia Stock Exchange firms classified as consumer cyclicals or consumer non-cyclicals during 2020–2024. Purposive screening produced 100 eligible firms and 500 balanced firm-year observations. Panel regression selected the Common Effect Model, followed by mean-centered moderated regression and diagnostic tests. Results: Audit quality is negatively associated with fraudulent financial reporting risk, whereas financial target and external pressure are positively associated with it. The other fraud-diamond proxies are not significant. Audit committee activity strengthens the protective association of audit quality and weakens the positive association of financial target but does not moderate the remaining relationships. Conclusion: Pressure-related factors are the dominant significant fraud-diamond signals in this sample, while the audit committee operates as a selective complement to external audit rather than a universal safeguard.

title: Risk committees and corporate disclosure: Evidence on risk and sustainability reporting with governance moderation
summary: Environmental and social concerns related to sustainability can represent non-financial risks requiring effective risk management (Wong, 2014). In this context, risk committees may play a role in overseeing such risks and their related corporate disclosures. This study investigates how risk committees impact both risk and sustainability disclosure, aiming to understand how corporate governance enhances transparency and investor confidence. It also examines whether board size, independence, and institutional ownership moderate these relationships, influencing the effectiveness of risk committees in corporate reporting. Using a quantitative approach, this study analyzed 807 samples from Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) companies that published sustainability reports between 2019 and 2023. The results show that risk committees positively influence risk disclosure but do not significantly affect sustainability disclosure. Moderation analysis indicates that board size and independence weaken the effect on risk disclosure. Conversely, institutional ownership strengthens the impact on sustainability disclosure, but not on risk disclosure. These findings suggest risk committees are more effective for traditional risk reporting than for sustainability transparency. This study provides new insights by testing the effectiveness of risk committees in enhancing both types of disclosures. It offers practical insights for regulators, investors, and corporate leaders, underscoring the importance of risk committees in improving disclosure quality to foster transparency and trust.

title: Human-Computer Interaction Insights from Web Portals in Consumer Banking
summary: The rapid digitalization of banking services has transformed the way consumers interact with financial institutions. Web portals, once limited to basic account inquiries, have evolved into comprehensive platforms offering seamless, secure, and personalized banking experiences. The effectiveness of these platforms largely depends on principles of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), which shape usability, accessibility, trust, and overall user satisfaction. This manuscript investigates the role of HCI in consumer banking portals, analyzing how design choices, user interface (UI) patterns, and interaction models influence customer engagement and service adoption. Drawing upon cross-disciplinary literature from information systems, behavioral finance, and interaction design, the paper highlights critical factors such as usability, personalization, accessibility, and cognitive load in shaping user experiences. The study further examines empirical findings from consumer banking contexts to identify design best practices and challenges. Results demonstrate that banking portals that prioritize intuitive design, adaptive personalization, and security transparency significantly enhance customer trust and loyalty. The manuscript contributes both theoretical insights and practical frameworks for improving banking portal design, bridging the gap between HCI theory and real-world financial technology (FinTech) applications.

title: Sustainable Development and Foreign Direct Investment: An Environmental, Social and Governance Perspective Based on the Sustainable Development Goal
summary: This study examines the relationship between environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance and foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows across countries, with particular attention to the individual ESG pillars. The analysis covers 189 countries over 2011–2025, using period averages to construct a cross-sectional dataset. ESG performance is derived from Sustainable Development Goal indicators and analyzed both as an aggregate index and through its environmental, social, and governance pillars. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and ordinary least squares regression with macroeconomic controls are employed. The aggregate ESG index is not significantly associated with FDI inflows. Governance is negatively and significantly associated with FDI, while the environmental pillar is positive but insignificant in the main model and becomes significant after excluding two influential observations. The social pillar remains insignificant. Overall, the results indicate substantial heterogeneity across ESG dimensions.

title: Does Institutional Quality Determine Environmental Sustainability?
summary: ABSTRACT Environmental sustainability increasingly depends on the alignment between development strategies and institutional governance, yet empirical evidence on the role of institutional quality in shaping environmental degradation remains highly contested. While institutions are widely theorised as central to environmental governance, existing studies report mixed and sometimes contradictory findings. This study addresses this ambiguity through a comprehensive meta‐analysis of 792 effect sizes drawn from 134 empirical studies examining the relationship between institutional quality and environmental degradation. Using random‐effects models, multilevel mixed‐effects models, and Bayesian model averaging, the analysis evaluates the average association between institutional quality and environmental degradation while explicitly accounting for heterogeneity, study dependence and publication bias. The results indicate that, on average, stronger institutional quality is associated with lower environmental degradation, though this relationship is highly conditional. Subgroup analyses show that World Governance and Political Risk indices yield more robust negative associations than narrower or compositionally heterogeneous measures and that effects are stronger for ecological footprint than carbon emissions. Meta‐regression identifies infrastructure, technology, globalisation, foreign direct investment and regional context as key moderators. The findings suggest institutional quality functions as a conditioning framework rather than a uniform determinant of environmental outcomes.

title: Macroeconomic Determinants of Energy Consumption in BRICS+ Countries: Evidence from a Pooled Mean Group Autoregressive Distributed Lag Panel Approach
summary: Against the backdrop of shifting global energy balances, this study analyzes energy consumption within the BRICS+ countries, using a panel of eight countries that combines the founding members (Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa) with three newly admitted members (Egypt, Iran, and Saudi Arabia). The objective is to quantify the impacts of financial development, economic growth, trade openness, and urbanization on energy demand. Covering the 1990–2021 period, the empirical analysis leverages data from the World Bank and the IMF. Following unit root and cointegration testing, the Pooled Mean Group (PMG-ARDL) model is employed to simultaneously estimate homogeneous long-run relationships and heterogeneous short-run dynamics. The analysis is further enriched by the Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel causality tests. The empirical findings reveal that, in the long run, financial development, economic growth, and trade openness significantly stimulate energy consumption, with economic growth emerging as the most influential driver. Conversely, urbanization exerts a positive but statistically insignificant effect. In the short run, only economic growth and financial development actively influence energy demand. These results underscore the critical importance of fostering green finance, achieving energy-growth decoupling, promoting sustainable trade policies, and implementing efficient urban planning to effectively reconcile economic expansion with energy sustainability.

title: A urgência de uma governança ambiental transnacional׃ uma abordagem centrada na política da agenda climática global
summary: In this paper, we propose a reflection on transnational climate governance as a mechanism for implementing sustainable development. However, the paper discusses the current international system’s inability to articulate concrete public policies capable of dealing with the climate change scenario. From a methodological point of view, the research developed an interdisciplinary bibliographic review, conceiving a holistic dialogue between theoretical perspectives centered on the climate agenda (environmental governance), international public policy and environmental law. The results of the study focused on the criticism of the concept of national borders and their respective jurisdictions, as they have proven inadequate to develop effective models of public policies and regulatory guidelines aimed at consolidating the climate agenda, considering that the biosphere constitutes a unique and interconnected system, transcending the administrative borders of countries. Finally, the research highlights the ineffectiveness of public international law in addressing environmental impacts, since it lacks binding force and remains dependent on the unilateral wills of states, and above all, on the dynamics of the conflicts of government cycles.

title: Empirical Analysis of Economic Transformation in Indonesia
summary: Indonesia aspires to achieve high-income status and become the world’s fifth-largest economy by 2045, leveraging its natural resources, demographic advantages, and large domestic market. This study applies a descriptive, indicator-based analysis of secondary macroeconomic, trade, labor, and digital-economy data (2000-2024) from BPS-Statistics Indonesia, Bank Indonesia, ADB, IMF, World Bank, and related sources, combined with document analysis of Indonesia’s economic transformation programs, to identify barriers and strategic opportunities for inclusive and sustainable annual growth of 6-7%. The findings indicate ongoing premature deindustrialization, low labor productivity, and a weak private sector contribution, as well as insufficient technological adoption and limited participation in global value chains. Despite some shifts toward higher-value-added sectors, productivity and efficiency remain stagnant, while the quality of human capital, as reflected by declining PISA scores, constrains labor market competitiveness. Investment inefficiencies, limited diversification, and low trade openness further challenge the transformation process. The digital economy, though growing rapidly, lags behind regional peers, hindered by inadequate digital infrastructure and low digital literacy. Addressing these issues requires strengthening human capital development, promoting innovation, enhancing connectivity, improving logistics, and formulating integrated policies to foster high-value production and global market integration. If successfully implemented, these strategic reforms will enable Indonesia to achieve its transformation goals, ensuring resilient growth, quality employment, and global competitiveness.

title: Audit Committee Characteristics and Financial Reporting Quality in Kenyan Non-Commercial State Corporations: The Moderating Roles of Accounting-System Automation and Staff Competence
summary: This study examines associations between audit committee independence, diversity, financial competence, meeting practices and the audit-query ratio among non-commercial state corporations in Kenya. It also considers accounting system automation and staff competence as moderators. From 72 targeted corporations, 46 heads of internal audit responded (63.89%). All four committee characteristics were negatively correlated with the audit-query ratio (r = −0.352 to −0.451). Meeting practices showed the most consistent negative association across the reported regression models. The analysis contributes to public-sector accountability research by distinguishing audit-query exposure from broader financial reporting quality and by interpreting the available empirical evidence within its methodological limits. Keywords: audit committee independence; audit committee diversity; financial competence; audit committee meetings; public-sector accountability; financial reporting quality.

title: Analysis of the Effect of Big Data on Supply Chain Optimization: A Case Study of JD Logistics' Freight and Warehousing Operations
summary: In the context of the deep integration of the digital economy, supply chain management is confronted with challenges such as demand fluctuations and information asymmetry. Big data technology is emerging as the core driving force for the precise transformation of supply chains. This paper takes JD Logistics as the research object and systematically analyzes the application paths and optimization effects of big data in the e-commerce supply chain. The research starts from the characteristics of supply chain big data, summarizes the development process and technical architecture of JD Logistics, and focuses on the specific practices of big data in inventory management, intelligent warehousing operations, and delivery optimization. Through a combination of case analysis and literature research, it demonstrates the significant role of big data technology in reducing JD’s warehousing costs and improving delivery efficiency, with a single delivery cost decreasing by 8.5%, unit warehousing cost decreasing by 12%, and order fulfillment rate increasing to 97%. The study shows that the supply chain management driven by big data achieves the unity of cost reduction, efficiency improvement, and service quality enhancement, providing a feasible practical path for the digital transformation of e-commerce logistics enterprises.

title: "Designing a Sustainable and Innovative Revenue Model for Livestock Dung Based Products"
summary: This academic project presents the Livestock Waste Value-Based Revenue Model (LWVR Model), a circular economy and waste-to-wealth framework designed to monetize underutilized agricultural by-products. Rather than treating animal dung strictly as bulk farm manure, the model details the systematic collection, segregation, drying, and eco-friendly packaging of dung powders from cows, goats, sheep, and buffaloes, alongside value-added offerings like traditional pooja cow dung cakes and Gomutra. The report examines multi-channel digital distribution through e-commerce marketplaces (Amazon, Flipkart) and direct-to-consumer (D2C) channels targeting urban home gardeners, terrace farmers, and plant nurseries in Tier 1 and Tier 2 cities. Key business dimensions analyzed include practical supply chain execution, operational feasibility, farmer income generation, revenue diversification, cost structures, and competitive challenges.

title: What are the key priority areas of agrifood systems transformation? A participatory science study for research and action from the farmers’ perspective
summary: Agrifood systems transformation has been called on by agricultural development agenda setters across the industry; however, questions arise regarding areas in the agrifood system worthy of research prioritization. While farmers are the primary drivers of agrifood systems, they are often uninvolved in co-creating the research and policy agendas governing the transformation of the very industry they lead. Our study applied community-engaged research principles to identify priority areas for transforming agrifood systems from farmers' perspectives. Farmers (n = 86) from rural El Salvador participated in a multistep, iterative data collection process, which included an initial individual collection of up to 10 key questions relevant to agrifood systems transformation, followed by a researcher-driven analysis/organization/ranking of themes, and a final participant review and validation. 376 questions, condensed to 89, were identified and categorized into nine themes: Environment and Sustainability, Productivity, Economy and Finances, Technical Assistance and Support, Supply Chain, Social and Cultural Shifts, Workforce, Innovation and Technology, and Governance and Regulation. We recommend using these priorities to facilitate inclusive and equitable agrifood systems transformation in El Salvador, which considers the needs of all stakeholders, particularly farmers, through participatory methodologies. Future research should expand to additional geographic regions, as agrifood systems transformations should follow a place-based approach.

title: Implementasi Asas Otonomi Daerah Berdasarkan Undang-Undang Nomor 23 Tahun 2014 dalam Penanganan Kebakaran Hutan dan Lahan
summary: Forest and land fires (karhutla) remain a major environmental challenge in Indonesia. This study analyzes the implementation of the regional autonomy principle under Law Number 23 of 2014 on Regional Government in addressing forest and land fires, identifies the challenges faced by local governments, and assesses the effectiveness of regional autonomy in improving coordination, prevention, and mitigation. The research employs a normative juridical approach through library research on legislation, scientific literature, and official government data. The findings indicate that regional autonomy has enabled local governments to establish policies and institutions supporting fire management, including Regional Disaster Management Agencies (BPBD), Fire Control Task Forces, and community-based prevention programs. However, implementation faces obstacles such as limited budgets, human resources, and facilities, weak inter-agency coordination, and low public participation. Regional autonomy has improved coordination and emergency response, yet remains suboptimal due to continued dependence on central government support in technology, funding, and law enforcement. Therefore, strengthening local institutional capacity, cross-sectoral coordination, and community participation is essential for more effective and sustainable environmental governance.

title: Governing Decarbonisation Through Policy Experimentation: Layered Site Selection in China's Low‐Carbon Pilot Programme
summary: ABSTRACT Policy piloting is central to China's experimentalist approach to environmental governance. Pilot programmes often expand through multiple rounds, but the extant literature explores them as a whole, with how site selection criteria change during expansion underexamined. We conceptualise multi‐round policy piloting as a dynamic process in which testing error is layered onto testing correctness as a programme expands. Testing correctness favours sites that are able to demonstrate feasibility, whereas testing error broadens selection to settings that can reveal the limits of policy applicability. We examine China's Low‐Carbon Province and City (LCPC) pilot, the country's first large‐scale national decarbonisation experiment. Using Cox proportional hazards and piecewise constant exponential models, we analyse city‐level entry into pilot coverage across successive batches. Baseline comparisons show greater fiscal capacity among pilot cities in all batches. Regression results show that favourable implementation conditions are associated with pilot entry in the initial stage and remain relevant during expansion. Later‐round entry is associated with proximity to national benchmarks in energy intensity and industrial structure, suggesting that representativeness also informs selection of pilot sites during expansion. These findings shed light on the promise and the limits of policy experimentation in China's low‐carbon transition.

title: Do the Corporate Governance Framework Mechanism Affect Sustainability Reporting in Food Beverage Companies?
summary: This study aims to examine the influence of corporate governance mechanisms on sustainability reporting within food and beverage (F&B) companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange for the 2021–2024 period. The research is motivated by increasing stakeholder demands for transparency regarding environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosures, as well as the significance of sustainability reporting as a form of legitimacy for a company’s internal responsibilities—reflected in its business strategy and long-term sustainability. The study utilizes secondary data obtained from companies' financial and sustainability reports. Panel data regression analysis is employed to test the impact of the independent variables—specifically corporate governance mechanisms, comprising board size, the presence of female directors, independent directors, and foreign directors—on sustainability reporting. The findings indicate that corporate governance mechanisms do not influence the level of sustainability reporting. None of the governance variables were found to have a significant effect on promoting sustainability reporting within these companies. Consequently, the implementation of corporate governance roles, particularly within the F&B sector, has yet to effectively enhance sustainability reporting. Keywords: sustainability reporting; female, independent and foreign directors; ESC.

title: Green Digital Transition and Sustainable Technology Supply Chains in the Mediterranean
summary: The rapid expansion of the digital economy poses dual challenges for the Mediterranean region: managing the surging energy and cooling demands of cloud infrastructure and mitigating electronic waste (e-waste) within fragile coastal ecosystems. This paper adopts a comparative qualitative synthesis of publicly available corporate sustainability disclosures, institutional environmental evidence, scientific and policy literature, and European Union regulatory sources to examine how the corporate models of Microsoft Corporation and Apple Inc. interact with sustainability challenges in the Mediterranean context. By contrasting Microsoft’s cloud-first, R&D-driven infrastructure expansion with Apple’s globally distributed, supplier-heavy hardware production model, we analyze key environmental risk vectors – specifically Scope 3 emissions, water scarcity in data center cooling, and e-waste management under the EU Circular Economy Framework. Ultimately, the study offers actionable policy and managerial recommendations for implementing Green IT and sustainable supply chain practices across Southern Europe and the wider Mediterranean policy context.

title: AI-Enabled Climate and Environmental ESG Assurance: Digital Audit Evidence, Assurance Quality and Governance A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Climate and environmental ESG reports have been released at a faster rate than assurance work for these reports. Review of 19 studies published from 2020 to 2025 on AI-enabled climate and environmental ESG assurance. Assurance, audit evidence, verification, quality of assurance and governance are the subjects of this paper, not general ESG disclosures or sustainable finance. The synthesis shows that AI is most impactful when altering the evidentiary architecture of assurance; satellite observations, NLP-extracted disclosures, Scope 3 value-chain data, blockchain traces, and AI-based textual diagnostics are creating new forms of digitally processable audit evidence. According to the above, the quality of assurance is determined by the 'four Cs': characteristics, competence, content and corroboration; automation is insufficient. The paper builds an Evidence-to-Assurance-to-Governance framework and links the antecedent pressures, digital audit evidence, AI-enabled assurance procedures, assurance outcomes and governance controls. It is to provide an impetus for the discussion of general AI-for-ESG in the audit and assurance field.

title: An Integrated Three‐Phase Green Quality Function Deployment Framework for Evaluating Lean–Green Criteria Under Uncertainty
summary: ABSTRACT Manufacturers need decision models that translate environmental and customer requirements into operational priorities while integrating lean and green practices within a unified programme. This study develops and applies an integrated decision framework to identify, structure and prioritise lean–green manufacturing criteria and to examine how their relative importance changes as strategic requirements are translated into technical, environmental and operational priorities. An initial literature‐derived set of 15 criteria and 55 subcriteria was refined through expert screening to eight criteria and 42 subcriteria. Fuzzy analytic network process (FANP) was first used to capture interdependencies among the retained criteria and derive their network‐based priorities. These priorities were subsequently carried through three linked green quality function deployment (GQFD) matrices, sequentially relating lean–green criteria to gearbox technical characteristics, environmental requirements and lean enablers. The resulting lean‐enabler weights were then incorporated into interval VIKOR to obtain the final compromise priorities under uncertainty. FANP ranked workforce, environmental performance and process highest, whereas the final analysis placed supply chain, performance outcomes and environmental performance in the leading positions. This cross‐stage reordering shows that structural importance within an interdependent decision network does not necessarily translate directly into implementation priority and demonstrates the value of tracing how lean–green priorities are reconfigured across successive deployment stages.
